clue.text: Visible shell-like coat, perhaps, reduced in width

indicators.note: something reduced in a given dimension has lost it, so the letter standing for that dimension is dropped

parts.note: a coat is an example of outerwear

explanation.surface: Something shell-like and visible, maybe a coat, has been cut down to a narrower size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shell-like' is British slang for the ear (as in 'a word in your shell-like'); the visible part is the outer ear.
explanation.definitionFit: Shell-like is British slang for an ear, and the part you can see is the external one.

clue.text: Collection of countries beginning to fuse into a republic, cutting cost

indicators.note: one letter is put into the trimmed name of a country
cutting a word from the country's name means removing those letters

parts.note: Costa Rica is a Central American republic
the letters of cost are taken as written

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A fuse is lit as a group of nations is drawn into a republic, which cuts costs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cutting cost' removes COST from COSTA RICA, leaving ARICA; the F from 'beginning to fuse' goes into it.
explanation.definitionFit: A continent is a large landmass made up of many countries.

clue.text: Instrument changing that which follows lines

indicators.note: letters changing shift into a different arrangement

parts.note: in clue order the next clue is 4 down, so this phrase stands for that clue's solution, the delicate shade
RY is short for railway, a set of lines

explanation.surface: A device that alters whatever comes after the lines of a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that which follows lines' suggests a postscript, and PS + ALTER tempts, but it leaves a Y over. 'that which follows' is the next clue's answer, PASTEL, and 'changing' rearranges it into PSALTE.
explanation.definitionFit: A psaltery is an ancient plucked stringed instrument, rather like a zither.

clue.text: Delicate shade of fine glass on top of lamp

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece placed on another sits above it

parts.note: paste is a hard, brilliant glass used to make imitation gems

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter

explanation.surface: A soft colour comes from the fine glass fitted on top of a lamp.
explanation.walkthrough: PASTE is the glass of costume jewellery; 'on' puts it above the L from 'top of lamp'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastel is a soft, pale colour, the kind called a delicate shade.

clue.text: Singular old soccer star, not unknown to be an untidy sort

parts.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular

indicators.note: not followed by a thing means that thing is left out

parts.note: Johan Cruyff was a famous Dutch footballer of the 1970s
Y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A former football great, unique in his way, turns out to be a scruffy type.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the Y (a mathematical unknown) from CRUYFF and put S in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A scruff is a person who looks dishevelled and unkempt.

clue.text: Working-class material getting better

parts.note: cloth is fabric or material
to cap something is to better or outdo it

explanation.surface: A working-class person gets hold of some fabric and improves their lot.
explanation.walkthrough: The flat cap was the emblem of the British working man, so 'cloth-cap' is used as an adjective meaning working-class.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain the flat woollen cap symbolises manual labourers, so the phrase serves as an adjective for that social group.

clue.text: PM once upset a king, e.g. James I

indicators.note: upset letters are knocked over into a fresh order

parts.note: Lear is a legendary king, Shakespeare's tragic hero
Sid James was a British comic actor of the Carry On films

explanation.surface: A former prime minister has upset a monarch such as James I.
explanation.walkthrough: 'e.g. James I' looks like the Stuart king, but James is the comic actor Sid James, giving SID, and I stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Benjamin Disraeli was Victorian Britain's Conservative prime minister twice.

clue.text: Clear unedited broadcast having lost appeal

indicators.note: something broadcast is scattered widely, so the letters are scattered into a new order
having lost something means it is taken away from the word

parts.note: it is slang for sex appeal

explanation.surface: A raw, unedited programme goes out on air but has lost its charm.
explanation.walkthrough: Take IT out of UNEDITED and rearrange the remaining UNEDED.
explanation.definitionFit: To strip land or a body bare is to clear it of its covering.

clue.text: Screwed face up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom

parts.note: the dial of a clock or watch is its face

explanation.surface: A face scrunched up in a grimace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screwed' looks like a description of the face, but it is the definition, in the slang sense of having had sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are vulgar slang past participles for having had sexual intercourse.

clue.text: The same old turns covered by prison entertainer

indicators.note: being covered by something means being enclosed within it

parts.note: can is slang for prison

indicators.note: the letters turn round and are read backwards

parts.note: idem is Latin for the same, used in references

explanation.surface: The same old routines are put on for an audience behind bars by a performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' looks like a performer's acts but reverses the Latin for 'the same' plus O; 'covered by' puts that inside the slang word for prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A comedian is a performer who makes audiences laugh, a type of entertainer.

clue.text: A box I posted in the French Republic

indicators.note: something posted in a place is put within it

parts.note: la is French for the (feminine)
the box is British slang for television

explanation.surface: Someone sends a box off to France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'box' is British slang for television; 'posted in' puts the pieces inside the French feminine article.
explanation.definitionFit: Latvia is a Baltic state with a republican constitution.

clue.text: Bargain shrewdly? Alan wheedled amazingly

indicators.note: letters arranged amazingly are put in a surprising new order

explanation.surface: A man named Alan coaxed his way to an astonishingly good deal.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to scheme and negotiate cleverly, often unscrupulously, for advantage.

clue.text: This suppresses report of a piece

definitions.text: This suppresses report of a piece

parts.words: This suppresses report of a piece
parts.note: a piece is slang for a gun, and its report is the bang; a device on the barrel muffles it

explanation.surface: Something that hushes up the news of an article.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' and 'piece' read as journalism, but they are a gunshot and a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A muffling device fitted to a firearm's barrel deadens the noise of the shot.

clue.text: Left after supporter, briefly showing detachment

indicators.note: one piece comes after the other in the answer
a word used briefly is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: a patron is a backer or supporter

explanation.surface: A backer departs, showing a lack of emotional involvement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detachment' suggests aloofness, but it is a small military unit. PATRON loses its N, then L follows.
explanation.definitionFit: In military usage a detachment is a small unit sent out, such as a group on reconnaissance.

clue.text: Prepared sterile tip on some fishing gear

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the second
letters prepared are worked up into a new form
the tip of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Instructions for readying sterile points on some angling equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange STERILE, then add the S from 'tip on some' below it.
explanation.definitionFit: These are pronged spears used to catch fish such as salmon, so they count as angling equipment.

clue.text: Well-paid pro in confusion after rise on 4th of July

indicators.note: one piece follows straight on from another
one piece comes after the other
the fourth letter of the word is taken

parts.note: up means rising, as in prices going up
pie is printers' jargon for jumbled type, hence confusion

explanation.surface: A highly paid professional is flustered after a pay rise on Independence Day.
explanation.walkthrough: '4th of July' looks like the US holiday but gives the fourth letter of July. 'confusion' is printers' pie, a heap of jumbled type.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1980s term was a nickname for a young urban professional earning a high salary.

clue.text: Odd training for cooking finishing early, with end of lesson skipped

parts.note: PE is physical education, training at school

indicators.note: a skipped letter is passed over and left out
a word finishing early stops before its last letter

parts.note: culinary means relating to cooking

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Odd that cookery classes finish early and the end of the lesson is missed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finishing early' drops the last letter of the cooking adjective, and 'skipped' removes the final letter of 'lesson' from what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: The words are synonyms for strange or unusual.

clue.text: Perhaps more biased means of pinning things down?

definitions.meaning: comparative of skew, meaning slanted or biased; the perhaps flags the jokey coinage
a long pin or spike used to hold meat together while cooking

explanation.surface: Someone more prejudiced might find a way to nail things down.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense reads the word as skew plus -er, a comparative coined for the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Both readings fit: a comparative of skew, and a spit holding pieces of food in place.

clue.text: Awkward situation of disgusting wife wearing small slip

indicators.note: pieces wearing a garment are put inside it

parts.note: a slip of paper such as a ticket
icky is informal for disgusting

explanation.surface: A revolting wife is dressed in a skimpy slip, an embarrassing scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wearing' puts the inner pieces inside the outer ones, after the slip's first letter. The phrase is cricket: a drying, rain-soaked pitch that is hard to bat on.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, from a treacherous cricket pitch, means a difficult predicament.

clue.text: Keen horse stuck in bottom of Becher's Brook

indicators.note: the letter is stuck in among the others
in a down clue the bottom of a word is its last letter

parts.note: a rill is a small brook
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: An eager horse gets stuck at the foot of Becher's Brook in the Grand National.
explanation.walkthrough: Becher's Brook is a famous fence at the Grand National, Britain's great steeplechase. H goes between S and RILL.
explanation.definitionFit: Keen can describe a high, piercing sound, as a keening wail is.

clue.text: Briefly show how bum gets rush, by the sound of it

definitions.text: rush, by the sound of it

indicators.note: bum as an adjective means bad or faulty, so the letters are put wrong
the word used briefly loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A demonstration of how a backside gets a sudden rush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' cuts the last letter of 'show', and SHO with HOW is rearranged. 'bum' looks like a noun here but works as the slang adjective for bad.
explanation.definitionFit: The word imitates the noise of something rushing past, so it is a rush in sound form.

clue.text: Persuade upon abstinence, initially stopping "one over the eight"?

indicators.note: a letter stopping a word plugs a gap in it

parts.note: the cox sits in front of the eight oarsmen of a rowing eight, steering them

indicators.note: initially means the first letter is used

explanation.surface: Urging abstinence by trying to stop someone having one drink too many.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One over the eight' is British slang for being drunk, but here it is the cox of a rowing eight.
explanation.definitionFit: The two verbs share the sense of gently getting someone to do something.

clue.text: Busy, in a Herculean way?

parts.note: busy is slang for a detective; Agatha Christie's sleuth has the first name Hercule

explanation.surface: Someone working with the energy of Hercules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Busy' looks like hard work, but it is British slang for a detective, and 'Herculean' points to his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie's Belgian investigator is a detective whose first name is Hercule.

clue.text: Bugs getting you mostly down — E coli

indicators.note: something getting to you unsettles you, so the letters are unsettled into a new order
mostly means all but the last letter

explanation.surface: Infections like E coli really get you down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bugs' suggests germs like E coli, but the answer is garden creatures. DOW from 'mostly down' and E COLI are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: These small crustaceans are informally called bugs.

clue.text: Livingstone maybe runs in user without it

indicators.note: one letter is put in the middle of the word
without means these letters are removed

parts.note: an exploiter uses others
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: David Livingstone, perhaps, runs into someone who exploits others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without it' removes those two letters, leaving EXPLOER, and 'in' places the cricket abbreviation for runs inside.
explanation.definitionFit: David Livingstone was a Victorian Scottish traveller in Africa, an example of someone who charts unknown lands.

clue.text: One entering names for flight

indicators.note: one piece entering another goes inside it

parts.note: big names are stars, famous people
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A single name joins the list for a plane journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flight' suggests air travel, but it is a set of steps.
explanation.definitionFit: A flight is a series of steps between floors.
